blocks.text: Dear Mr. Smith:

This letter sets out the terms on which our firm will carry out a reputation audit for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}, and it becomes our agreement once you have countersigned and returned it. We have written it in plain terms, so that it reads as a fair record of the conversation we have had rather than as a document to be decoded. Where the language is careful, it is careful for your protection as much as for ours.

Please read it against your own understanding of what we discussed. If any line here sits at odds with that, tell us before you sign, and we will put it right together. Nothing in these pages is meant to surprise you later.
The Audit We Propose

We propose to examine how {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} is understood today by the audiences whose view of the company carries the most weight: its investors, the trade and financial press that cover it, and the people inside the company who speak for it. Our aim is a clear, evidence-based account of where the company's reputation is strong, where it is exposed, and where the distance between how the company sees itself and how it is seen runs widest.

The audit will draw on the company's recent public communications, the coverage those communications have attracted, and a set of confidential conversations with people you nominate. It does not extend to the running of the company or to decisions that are properly yours; where our findings touch those decisions, they remain findings, and the judgment stays with you.
How We Will Work

We begin by reading the record: the announcements, filings, and materials the company has issued, set beside the press and analyst commentary they drew. From there we listen, in a small number of confidential interviews with the executives and outside parties you point us to, so that what people actually believe is placed next to what the company has said about itself.

We then bring the two together into a written assessment, tested with you before it is final, that names the strengths worth protecting and the risks worth addressing. Because so much of this work moves by correspondence, we keep a clean record of what we send and route anything sensitive through a single point on each side, so that you always know where a given thread stands and never have to hunt for the current version.
The People on the Work

Michelle Rose will carry the engagement day to day and will be your first point of contact for anything of substance. She does the close work on the drafting and keeps the moving parts legible, and she is the person to bring a question to when it needs a quick answer.

Kimberly Le will handle the media and analyst review, reading how the company's story is moving across the coverage and compressing a noisy record into something you can act on. I will keep a hand on the work myself, and particularly on the sensitive findings; nothing of weight will leave our office under our name without my having read it. You are welcome to come to me directly at any time, though Michelle Rose will usually be the quicker route to an answer.
Fee and Start

Our fee for the audit is {{fact:f:E-2024-001.fee}}, covering the work described above through the delivery of our written assessment. The engagement will begin on {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}} and is expected to run about four months from that point, though we will treat it as finished when the work is genuinely done rather than when the calendar says so.
Fees and Payment

We will invoice against the fee as the work proceeds, and our invoices are payable within thirty days of receipt. The fee covers our people and their time; it does not cover out-of-pocket costs such as travel or third-party research, which we will agree with you before anything of consequence is incurred. Should the scope of the audit change materially, we will raise the matter with you and settle the fee before that additional work begins.
Term and Termination

Either of us may bring the engagement to a close on fourteen days' written notice. If you end it, you will owe us for the work properly completed to that point and for any costs already committed on your behalf, and nothing beyond that. We would, of course, hope to talk before it came to that.
Confidentiality

Everything we learn about {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} in the course of the audit we will hold in confidence and use only for this engagement. That obligation binds our whole team, survives the end of our work together, and covers the fact of our involvement as much as its substance. We ask the same of you for the methods and materials we share with you.
Limitation of Liability

We will carry out the audit with the care and skill you are entitled to expect, and we stand behind our work. We do not, however, control how the press, the markets, or other third parties will finally read the company, and so our liability to you under this engagement is limited to the fees paid under it, except in those respects where the law does not permit such a limit.
Governing Law

This agreement is governed by the law of the state in which our firm is established, and any dispute arising under it will be resolved in that state's courts. Should any single provision be found unenforceable, the remainder of this letter stands unaffected.

If this reflects our understanding, please countersign below and return one copy to us, keeping the other for your files. Once it is back with us, Michelle Rose will be in touch to arrange the first conversations and to ask for the materials we will need to begin. We are glad to be starting this work with the Gallegos, Pope and Marsh team.

We are under way on the reputation audit for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}, with our start set at {{fact:f:E-2024-001.start}}. The job is to establish how the company is seen by its investors, by the press that covers it, and by its own people, and to set that reading against how the company describes itself. The gap between the two, wherever it turns out to be widest, is what the audit is really after. This note lays out who is carrying what in the opening weeks, so nothing waits on a handoff that was never made.

A word first on how we keep it in order. We hold the correspondence clean, route anything client-facing through one point, and log what we send, so the record stays legible as the volume builds. None of that is new to us, but it is worth saying once at the start of a job that will live mostly in email, and it matters more here because much of what we gather will be said to us in confidence.

Kimberly Le takes the media and analyst review. She is pulling the coverage from the last two years and reading how the company's story has moved through it, so we know what the outside record actually says before we ask anyone inside about it. Her first task is to sort that coverage into the themes that recur, and to flag the places where the reporting and the company's own account pull apart. Those themes will also shape the questions we carry into the interviews.

I am carrying the interview program. We will run a short set of confidential conversations with the executives and a few outside parties, and I will build the list and the question set this week. These conversations sit at the center of the audit, so we want them scheduled early rather than left to the end, when calendars tighten and people travel. I will keep each one to under an hour and send the questions ahead, so no one is asked to think on their feet about a hard subject.

We will meet briefly each week to compare what the coverage is showing against what the interviews are turning up, and to adjust the questions as we go. Kimberly Le and I will keep our notes in the shared file rather than in our inboxes, so either of us can pick up where the other left off. If either track runs ahead or behind, we will say so early rather than let it surface at the end.

We also need the company's own materials: the recent announcements, the investor decks, and anything else that shapes how the company is read. Robert Smith is our single contact for that on the Gallegos, Pope and Marsh side, and every request for access or scheduling goes to him rather than out across their team. That keeps one clean thread on the client's side and spares them fielding the same question three different ways.

The first thing that has to happen is the interview list. I will circulate a draft by the end of the week; send me any names you think belong on it before then, so we go to Robert Smith with one considered request rather than a trickle of them.
Hello Robert,

I wanted to open a thread to keep us current on the reputation audit for {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}, so the updates and any questions stay in one place as we go. We are a few weeks in now and moving on two fronts at once, and so far the picture is taking shape roughly as we expected.

Kimberly Le has finished the first pass through the recent coverage and the analyst notes, and she is now sorting what she found into the themes that come up most often. Alongside that, we are ready to begin the confidential interviews, and I have a short list of the internal people we would like to speak with. Where any of them sit outside your own group, a quick word from you to clear the introduction would help us reach them.

The one thing we need from your side to hold this pace is the last set of investor materials, meaning the most recent deck and any messaging you have used since the fall. I will keep these requests coming to you directly, Robert Smith, rather than spread across the Gallegos, Pope and Marsh team, so nothing gets lost between desks. Send them whenever they are to hand and we will take the next step from there.
Thanks
Robert,

To add to Michelle Rose's note, the coverage review is now in reasonable shape. I have read the last two years of trade and financial press, together with the analyst commentary, and sorted it into a handful of recurring themes.

Two points are worth raising early, with the usual caution that a first read can still shift. The Gallegos, Pope and Marsh operational record is covered fairly and consistently, which is a real strength. The financial narrative, by contrast, is told less clearly, and where it is thin a few outlets fill the gap with framing of their own. Neither point is a conclusion yet; both are early reads that the interviews will test.

It would help to see the investor materials before I take this any further, so that I can set what {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} has said against how it has been received. I will hold the fuller write-up until those are to hand, Robert Smith. A day or two either way makes little difference; having the documents in front of me makes a great deal.
Best
Hello Robert,

Thanks for this. To keep the audit moving, I have three of the internal interviews penciled in for next week and am waiting on two more to confirm. Once those last two land, I will send you the full schedule in a single note, so you can see the whole set at once rather than in pieces.

Kimberly Le will fold her coverage read into the same interviews, so we ask each person about the themes the press has raised rather than running the two tracks apart. That keeps the conversations short and pointed, which I know matters for the people you are lending us.

The one open item is still the investor materials Kimberly asked about. If those reach us before the interviews begin, we go into each conversation already knowing what {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}} has said publicly, which spares your people fielding the same questions twice. I will keep these requests coming to you directly, Robert Smith, rather than across the Gallegos, Pope and Marsh team. Send them when you can and we will build the rest around them.
Thanks
Robert,

Following Michelle Rose's note, I will have a short brief ready for each interview, so that the person you are lending us sees the themes ahead of the conversation rather than meeting them cold. Each brief runs to a page. I will keep them plain.

For the audit of {{fact:f:E-2024-001.client}}, the worth of these conversations rests on that preparation. The coverage gives us the outside view; the interviews give us the inside one; the two belong side by side before I draw any conclusion. Read on its own, either one can mislead.

That returns me to the investor materials. Once they are in hand, I can align each brief to what the company has actually said, so that the Gallegos, Pope and Marsh interviews do not spend their hour on ground the documents already cover. I will send the briefs to you first, Robert Smith, so you can look them over before your people do.
Best
